# OPENING STATEMENT FOR THE PROSECUTION

**IN THE HIGH COURT OF THE REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA**

**Case No.: HC/ALU/2026/____**

**The State v. A. Bandara**

---

May it please Your Lordship,

I appear for the State, and on the State's behalf I now open the case against the accused, A. Bandara, who stands indicted on a charge of **voluntarily causing grievous hurt, contrary to Section 324 of the Penal Code**.

---

## The Charge

The accused is charged that, on the date in question, at the town market, he did voluntarily cause grievous hurt to the complainant, namely a fractured arm, by striking the complainant with a wooden crate. Section 324 carries a maximum sentence of imprisonment up to seven years and a fine.

The State will also demonstrate, at the close of evidence, that the lesser alternative under Section 326 — voluntarily causing grievous hurt on provocation — does not avail the accused on the facts, and that the principal charge under Section 324 is squarely made out.

---

## The Facts the State Will Prove

The evidence will establish the following sequence of events beyond reasonable doubt:

1. **The Setting.** On a market day, a dispute arose between two vendors — the complainant and the accused — over the boundary of a stall.

2. **The Escalation.** That dispute escalated into a physical confrontation. Two independent bystanders, who observed both the inception of the argument and its escalation, will testify to what they saw.

3. **The Act.** The accused struck the complainant with a wooden crate. That crate, recovered at the scene, will be produced before this Court as an exhibit.

4. **The Injury.** The blow caused a fracture of the complainant's arm. The hospital admission record, generated in the ordinary course of medical treatment, will formally establish the nature and gravity of the injury. The complainant was hospitalised for ten days before discharge.

---

## The Legal Elements the State Must Establish, and Will Establish

To secure a conviction under Section 324, the State must prove, and undertakes to prove, four elements:

**(a) Voluntariness.** The act of striking the complainant with a wooden crate was a voluntary, conscious act on the part of the accused. It was not accidental, not reflexive in any lawful sense, and not the product of automatism. A man who picks up a crate and swings it at another person acts voluntarily.

**(b) Intention or Knowledge.** The accused either intended to cause the hurt, or knew that the hurt was likely to be caused. Striking a human body with a hard wooden object, delivered with force sufficient to fracture bone, is conduct from which the necessary mens rea is plainly inferable. The State will rely on the well-settled principle that intention may, and often must, be inferred from the nature of the weapon used, the force employed, and the part of the body struck.

**(c) The Causing of Hurt.** "Hurt" is defined under Section 311 of the Penal Code, and a fracture of the arm plainly falls within that definition.

**(d) Grievous Hurt.** Section 311, read with the relevant clauses, classifies as "grievous" any hurt which amounts to a fracture of a bone. The State will prove, through the hospital record, that a bone — the arm — was fractured.

---

## The Defence Theory, and Why It Fails

The State anticipates that the defence will contend that the blow was struck in the heat of a sudden quarrel, without premeditation. The State concedes, for the purposes of this opening, that the altercation was a sudden one. The State **denies** that this assists the accused in the manner the defence may suggest, for two reasons:

**First**, a sudden quarrel is not, of itself, a defence to a charge under Section 324. Section 324 punishes the voluntary causing of grievous hurt. What it does not require is premeditation. The accused need not have planned the assault; it is enough that he chose, in the moment, to swing a wooden crate at another human being with force sufficient to break bone.

**Second**, the defence of provocation, which is the only route by which the suddenness of the quarrel might reduce the charge, is governed by Section 326 itself and by the principles laid down in our jurisprudence. The State will demonstrate that, even taking the defence at its highest, what occurred was no mere exchange of heated words culminating in a momentary loss of self-control. The accused armed himself with a wooden crate — an object of considerable weight and rigidity — and used it as a weapon against a fellow vendor over a stall boundary. The State will invite this Court to hold that this conduct falls well outside the ambit of Section 326, and squarely within Section 324.

---

## The Evidence the State Will Adduce

In support of its case, the State will call the following evidence:

1. **The testimony of two bystander witnesses**, who observed the argument begin and escalate, and who will speak to the accused's conduct and the use of the wooden crate.

2. **The hospital admission record** of the complainant, which documents the fracture of the arm and the ten-day period of hospitalisation.

3. **The wooden crate** itself, recovered at the scene, to be produced and identified.

4. **The medical and circumstantial inference** arising from the nature of the weapon and the injury, which the State will submit to this Court as establishing both the manner of the assault and the requisite mental element.

---

## The State's Submissions in Summary

The State will prove, to the requisite standard, that on a market day, in the course of a dispute over a stall boundary, the accused took up a wooden crate and struck the complainant with it; that the blow was voluntary and intentional in the legal sense; that it caused a fracture of the complainant's arm; and that such a fracture constitutes grievous hurt within the meaning of the Penal Code.

The State will accordingly invite this Honourable Court to return a finding of guilt on the charge under Section 324 of the Penal Code.

---

I thank Your Lordship. The State calls its first witness.

# OPENING STATEMENT FOR THE DEFENCE

**IN THE HIGH COURT OF THE REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA**

**Case No.: HC/ALU/2026/____**

**The State v. A. Bandara**

---

May it please Your Lordship,

I appear for the accused, A. Bandara, and on his behalf I now open the defence case. Before the evidence unfolds, I wish to place before this Honourable Court the framework within which the defence invites the learned Judge to evaluate the prosecution's case, and the considerations that must weigh in the accused's favour both on the question of guilt and, if guilt be found, on the question of sentence.

---

## I. THE BURDEN REMAINS ON THE STATE

The defence begins with a foundational principle of our criminal law, codified in the **Evidence Ordinance (Cap. 14)**, and reinforced in a long line of decisions of our superior courts: the burden of proving the guilt of the accused rests, throughout the trial, upon the prosecution. That burden is **never shifted**. The accused is presumed innocent. He need not prove his innocence; the State must disprove it, **beyond reasonable doubt**.

The defence will listen carefully to the evidence led by the State. Where that evidence falls short, the defence will say so. Where it is contradicted, the defence will so submit. The accused is not required to establish the truth of any alternative narrative; he is entitled to the benefit of every reasonable doubt that the evidence may generate.

---

## II. THE CONCESSIONS THE DEFENCE MAKES, AND THE ONUS THAT REMAINS

To be candid with the Court, the defence makes the following concessions at the outset, in the interests of a fair and orderly trial:

1. That a dispute arose between the accused and the complainant on a market day concerning a stall boundary.
2. That the accused struck the complainant.
3. That the complainant sustained a fracture of the arm and was hospitalised for ten days.

These concessions, however, are **not concessions of guilt on the charge as framed**. They are concessions of selected factual circumstances, stripped of the legal characterisation the State seeks to place upon them. The defence denies that these circumstances, when properly understood and weighed in light of the law, establish the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt under Section 324 beyond reasonable doubt.

---

## III. THE DEFENCE CASE IN SUMMARY

The accused's case, in its essential features, is this:

**A. The Quarrel Was Sudden and the Blow Unpremeditated.**

The accused did not attend the market that day with any intention of confronting the complainant. The dispute was a spontaneous one — a verbal disagreement over a stall boundary that escalated with the kind of rapidity that is, unhappily, common in crowded market settings. The accused's plea from the outset has been that the blow was struck in the heat of a sudden quarrel, without prior planning.

This fact, taken with the other circumstances, is of direct legal relevance. While the State correctly observes that premeditation is not an element of Section 324, the **absence of premeditation**, combined with the **suddenness of the quarrel** and the **emotional context in which the blow was struck**, is highly material — both to the proper characterisation of the mental element, and to the question of which provision of the Penal Code, between Sections 324 and 326, is properly engaged.

**B. The Mental Element Is at the Heart of This Case.**

The State has, in its opening, treated the mental element as something to be "inferred" from the weapon and the injury. The defence submits that the State cannot discharge its burden by inference alone, where the actual evidence of what occurred tells a different story.

A man who, in a moment of heated exchange, swings an object at his adversary, is not necessarily a man who either intended to cause grievous hurt, or knew that grievous hurt was likely. The distinction between intending to cause hurt and intending to cause grievous hurt is a distinction the law recognises and respects. The defence will invite this Court to consider, on the totality of the evidence, whether the accused possessed the requisite mental state for the offence charged, or whether his conduct falls within a lesser legal category.

**C. Section 326 Is Engaged on These Facts.**

The defence will submit that the proper charge on the facts, if any charge is made out at all, is **voluntarily causing grievous hurt on provocation, contrary to Section 326 of the Penal Code**, and not the principal charge under Section 324.

The ingredients of Section 326 are well established, and on the evidence as the defence anticipates it, each is satisfied:

- The accused caused grievous hurt (a fracture);
- He did so voluntarily;
- He did so **on grave and sudden provocation**.

The provocation in this case is the sudden and unanticipated dispute over the stall boundary — a matter of immediate economic concern to the accused, a working vendor — which escalated rapidly in a public, crowded, and emotionally charged environment. The defence will say, with respect, that the State cannot succeed in sidelining Section 326 by characterising the accused's conduct as "armouring himself" with a crate. The crate was the object to hand, in a market, in the middle of an argument. To elevate its use into evidence of a heightened mens rea is, the defence submits, a distortion of the facts and of the law.

The defence further notes that the State, in its opening, has purported to "anticipate" the defence and to "deny" that Section 326 applies. With respect, that is a matter for this Court to determine on the evidence, and not for the State to pre-judge. The prosecution's anticipation of the defence is not evidence; it is argument. The defence will meet that argument on its merits, in due course.

---

## IV. EVIDENTIARY CHALLENGES THE DEFENCE RESERVES

The defence reserves the right to raise the following matters at the appropriate stage of the trial:

**1. The Wood Crate as an Exhibit.**

The State has indicated it will produce the wooden crate as an exhibit. The defence will scrutinise the chain of custody, the identification of the object, and the manner in which it was recovered. An object whose provenance and continuity of possession are not properly established is of little, if any, probative value.

**2. The Hospital Record.**

The defence does not contest that the complainant was treated for a fracture, but reserves the right to cross-examine on the precise nature and extent of the injury, the treatment given, and any relevant clinical observations. The mere fact of a fracture, while it satisfies the definition of grievous hurt, does not by itself establish how that fracture was caused, or by whom.

**3. The Bystander Witnesses.**

The State has referred to "two independent bystanders." The defence will test that characterisation. Independence is not a label that witnesses acquire by the prosecution's description of them; it is a quality to be examined. The defence will cross-examine these witnesses with care and with the respect due to the Court, on what they claim to have seen and heard, on the positions from which they observed, on the duration and quality of their observation, and on any prior connection with the complainant.

**4. The Absence of Forensic or Corroborative Evidence.**

The defence notes, without at this stage making formal submissions, that the State appears to rely on a relatively thin evidentiary base — two bystander accounts, a hospital record, and the weapon itself. The defence will invite this Court, in accordance with long-standing principle, to weigh oral testimony with appropriate caution, and to require the strict proof that the law demands before a conviction can rest.

---

## V. MITIGATING FACTORS THE DEFENCE WILL PLACE BEFORE THE COURT

Should the matter proceed to sentence — and the defence emphasises that guilt must first be established beyond reasonable doubt — the defence will invite the Court to take the following matters into account:

1. **The accused has no prior convictions**, a matter of which the Court will be formally apprised at the appropriate stage.

2. **The accused is a working vendor** of long standing, with no known history of violence. The incident must be understood in the context of a sudden, situational dispute, and not as part of any pattern of conduct.

3. **The provocation, though not a defence in the technical sense to Section 324, is highly relevant to sentence.** A man who loses his self-control in the heat of a sudden quarrel stands in a different moral position from one who carries a weapon to a place with the intention of using it.

4. **The accused has no connection to organised violence or criminal enterprise.** This was a dispute between two working people over a working matter, in a working place.

5. **The accused is, on the information presently available, a man of previously good character, with family responsibilities and a contribution to make to the economic life of his community.** The defence will place evidence of these matters before the Court in due course, through sworn testimony and, if appropriate, through the reports of the Probation Officer under the provisions of the **Children and Young Persons Ordinance** and the **Probation of Offenders Ordinance** framework, in so far as it may be applicable to an adult accused.

6. **The relationship of the incident to Section 326 is, in itself, a mitigating circumstance.** The fact that the lawmaker has seen fit to provide a lesser offence, with a lesser maximum penalty, for conduct of this character is itself a legislative recognition that such conduct is differently situated from conduct falling squarely within Section 324.

---

## VI. THE DEFENCE'S POSITION IN SUMMARY

The defence's position may be summarised as follows:

- The State bears the burden of proving every element of the offence charged, beyond reasonable doubt.
- The State must prove, and not merely infer, the mental element for Section 324.
- On the facts as the defence understands them, the mental element for the principal charge is not made out; the conduct of the accused, if culpable at all, falls within Section 326.
- The State cannot, by means of rhetorical characterisation in its opening, convert a sudden quarrel into a calculated assault, or convert a wooden crate to hand into a chosen weapon.
- The accused is entitled to the presumption of innocence, the benefit of every reasonable doubt, and the full application of the law as it stands — including the law of provocation and the lesser charge under Section 326.
- Should sentence be reached, the accused is entitled to the consideration of this Court on the mitigating factors to which I have referred.

The defence will, in the course of the trial, test the prosecution's evidence rigorously but fairly, will present such evidence as the accused may be advised to place before the Court, and will at all times assist the Court in the search for the truth.

---

## VII. PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION ON PROCEDURE

Before the defence witnesses — should any be called — or the accused himself takes the stand, the defence wishes to place on record the following:

The accused is entitled, by the Constitution of the Republic of Sri Lanka — in particular **Article 13(2), which guarantees the right to a fair trial**, and the long line of authority thereunder — to a full and fair opportunity to meet the case against him. The defence will conduct this case with that constitutional entitlement firmly in mind, and trusts that the prosecution will do the same.

---

May it please Your Lordship, the defence has now opened its case. I thank Your Lordship for the patience with which this opening has been received.

I shall now, with Your Lordship's leave, proceed to cross-examine the witnesses called by the State.

---

*Respectfully submitted on behalf of the accused, A. Bandara.*

**Defense Counsel**
*For the Accused*

# SUBMISSION ON BEHALF THE PROSECUTION

## STAGE: PRESENTATION OF EVIDENCE

*In the High Court of Sri Lanka*
*Case No: __________*
*King v. A. Bandara*

---

May it please Your Honour,

I appear for the State, and at this stage I shall present the evidence in support of the charge under Section 324 of the Penal Code. I will move through the evidence in three logical steps: first, the witnesses who saw the altercation unfold; second, the medical record confirming the injury sustained; and third, the recovered weapon — the wooden crate — which connects the accused to the act. Each piece, I submit, corroborates the next, and together they establish every element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt.

---

### I. THE EYEWITNESS ACCOUNT

I propose to call the two bystanders, who were present at the market and observed the dispute from its inception.

Their evidence will be consistent in the following material particulars:

1. **The genesis of the dispute** — On the market day in question, the accused and the victim were both vendors operating adjacent stalls. A disagreement arose concerning the boundary of their respective stalls. This is the ordinary backdrop to the offence and matters, because it shows the quarrel was over a *trivial matter of the moment*, not some pre-existing vendetta — a fact the Defence will undoubtedly emphasise, but which, as I will later submit in law, does not diminish culpability under Section 324.

2. **The escalation** — The witnesses will describe how the verbal exchange escalated, with raised voices, but importantly, **without any physical confrontation being initiated by the victim**. The accused is the one who took the dispute from words to violence.

3. **The act itself** — The accused picked up a wooden crate and struck the victim with it. The blow was direct, deliberate, and forceful. The witnesses will say — and I quote the anticipated substance of their testimony — that the accused "swung the crate at" the victim and struck the victim's arm. This is not a push, not a slap, not an instinctive flailing; it is the use of an implement as a weapon.

4. **The immediacy of response** — The victim collapsed, clutching his arm. The fracture was audible and visible. The witnesses summoned assistance, and the victim was taken to hospital.

The Defence will no doubt invite the Court to accept the accused's version — that the blow was struck "in the heat of a sudden quarrel and without prior planning." I do not dispute that. I **concede** that the quarrel was sudden and that there was no premeditation. But, with respect, that concession is legally irrelevant to the charge under Section 324, as I shall set out when I address you on the law. For now, I simply note: the witnesses' account is what Your Honour must weigh, and it is a clear, forthright, and unembellished description of a deliberate act of violence.

I will also respectfully draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that there is no allegation, no suggestion from any witness, and no evidence that the victim struck first, brandished any object, or otherwise created a situation in which the accused was compelled to defend himself. This is not a case where the Defence can invoke the right of private defence under Section 32 of the Penal Code, nor can they meaningfully anchor a provocation argument under Section 326 — and I will return to this in my submissions on the law.

---

### II. THE MEDICAL EVIDENCE

I next invite the Court to receive the hospital admission record of the victim.

The record will prove the following:

1. **The injury** — The victim was admitted with a **fracture of the arm**. The medical documentation is conclusive on this point; it is a finding made by qualified medical professionals in the ordinary course of their duty, and it is the very type of record the Courts of this country have long received without challenge to its accuracy.

2. **The nature and gravity of the injury** — A fracture is, by its very nature, a **grievous injury** as defined under Section 311 of the Penal Code. Section 311 expressly provides that the following kinds of hurt are designated as "grievous":

   *"(First) — Emasculation;*
   *(Secondly) — Permanent privation of the sight of either eye;*
   *(Thirdly) — Permanent privation of the hearing of either ear;*
   *(Fourthly) — Privation of any member or joint;*
   *(Fifthly) — Destruction or permanent impairment of the powers of any member or joint;*
   *(Sixthly) — Permanent disfiguration;*
   *(Seventhly) — Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth;"*

   The hospital record directly engages the **seventh clause**. A fractured arm is a textbook instance of "grievous hurt" within the statutory definition. There is no need for the Prosecution to engage in any extended argument on this limb; the medical record speaks for itself.

3. **Treatment and duration** — The victim was hospitalised for **ten (10) days** before being discharged. This period of treatment is a further indicator, if one were needed, of the seriousness of the injury inflicted. It corroborates the fact that the harm caused was not transient or trivial.

I pause here to emphasise a point that is sometimes overlooked: the Prosecution does not have to prove that the accused *intended* to cause grievous hurt. The offence under Section 324 requires only that the accused **voluntarily caused** grievous hurt. The voluntariness of the act is established by the witnesses; the grievous nature of the hurt is established by the medical record. The elements are made out.

---

### III. THE RECOVERED WEAPON

I now turn to the third item of evidence: the **wooden crate recovered at the scene**.

The crate is a physical object capable of being produced before Your Honour. Its relevance is twofold:

1. **Identification and connection to the accused** — The crate is the very implement described by the eyewitnesses as having been used by the accused. It was recovered at the scene of the altercation, in close proximity to where the victim fell. The chain of custody, which I am prepared to establish through the investigating officer if required, links the crate to the accused's act.

2. **Nature of the instrument used** — A wooden crate, swung with force against a human arm, is plainly an object capable of causing — and in this case, *did* cause — a fracture. This is not a case of bare-handed contact; it is a case of the accused arming himself, even momentarily, with a hard, blunt, heavy object and using it as a weapon. This bears directly on the question of the *manner* in which the hurt was inflicted, and is highly relevant — should Your Honour be minded to consider the question of sentence — as an aggravating circumstance.

I will formally move that the crate be marked as an exhibit and produced for the Court's inspection.

---

### IV. THE CONSISTENCY OF THE EVIDENCE

With Your Honour's leave, I wish to step back and observe the **architecture** of the case for the prosecution. Three independent sources of evidence converge:

| Element of the Offence | Evidence Establishing It |
|---|---|
| The act of causing hurt | Eyewitness testimony of two bystanders |
| The weapon used | The recovered wooden crate |
| The grievous nature of the injury | Hospital admission record (fracture of the arm) |

No single piece of evidence stands alone. Each corroborates the other. The witnesses speak of a blow; the medical record confirms a fracture consistent with a blow from a hard object; the crate is the hard object. This is, in the Prosecution's submission, a coherent, mutually-corroborating body of evidence. There is no material inconsistency, no contradiction, and no suggestion of fabrication.

The Defence's case, as foreshadowed in the case file, rests solely on the accused's own assertion that the blow was struck "in the heat of a sudden quarrel." I make two observations on this: first, the assertion is not, in itself, *evidence* in the strict sense — it is the accused's account, which Your Honour will weigh as such; and secondly, even if accepted in its entirety, it does not, in law, amount to a defence to a charge under Section 324. I will develop this fully in my submissions on the law.

---

### V. ORDER OF WITNESSES AND EXHIBITS

For the orderly conduct of proceedings, I propose the following sequence:

1. **First bystander** — examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination.
2. **Second bystander** — examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination.
3. **Production and proof of the hospital admission record** — through the investigating officer or by formal proof under the relevant provisions, with a medical practitioner available if the Defence requires clarification.
4. **Production and identification of the wooden crate** — through the investigating officer, with proof of chain of custody.
5. **Such further evidence as the Court may permit**, depending on the course of the Defence case.

---

### VI. CONCLUSION OF THIS STAGE

In summary at this stage, the Prosecution has presented, and will continue to present, evidence that:

- The accused, in a sudden quarrel over a stall boundary, **deliberately picked up a wooden crate and struck the victim** with it;
- The blow caused a **fractured arm** — a grievous injury within the meaning of Section 311, seventh clause, of the Penal Code;
- The injury required **ten days of hospitalisation**;
- The instrument used was a **wooden crate**, recovered at the scene, which the eyewitnesses identify as the weapon employed.

The voluntary nature of the act is established. The grievous nature of the hurt is established. The act and the hurt are causally connected. The charge under Section 324 is made out on the evidence.

I respectfully invite Your Honour to receive this evidence and to weigh it in due course against whatever the Defence may advance. I will address Your Honour on the legal elements of the offence, and on the question of whether any lesser or alternative view of the facts could displace the charge under Section 324, at the appropriate stage.

I am obliged, Your Honour.

**State Counsel**
*For the Prosecution*
*High Court of Sri Lanka*

# IN THE HIGH COURT OF [DISTRICT]

**Case No. [____]**
**The Republic v. A. Bandara**

---

## SUBMISSION ON BEHALF OF THE ACCUSED

### I. INTRODUCTION

The Defence, appearing for the Accused, A. Bandara, rises pursuant to the stage of **defence evidence** to present its case. The Prosecution alleges that the Accused committed the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, contrary to Section 324 of the Penal Code, in that the Accused struck the victim with a wooden crate, fracturing the latter's arm.

The Defence does not contest the occurrence of the injury. The Defence, however, denies the requisite *mens rea* for the offence charged. We shall proceed to outline our legal position, the evidence we propose to lead, and the mitigating factors this Honourable Court is invited to weigh in considering sentence.

---

### II. ISSUES FOR DETERMINATION

1. Whether the Prosecution has proved, beyond reasonable doubt, that the Accused acted with the specific intention required under Section 324 of the Penal Code.
2. Whether the act falls within the lesser offence of voluntarily causing hurt (Section 322) or the exception of sudden quarrel under the Fourth Exception to Section 300 (read with the general exceptions in Chapter IV of the Penal Code).
3. The appropriate sentence, should the Court be satisfied that the offence is made out.

---

### III. THE PROSECUTION'S CASE

The Prosecution's case, as understood from the indictment and the statement of facts, is that on a market day, a dispute arose between two vendors over a stall boundary; the argument escalated; and the Accused struck the victim with a wooden crate, fracturing the victim's arm. The victim was hospitalised for ten days.

The Defence notes that the Prosecution has not produced any weapon, photographs of the scene, or independent eyewitness evidence. The sole account before the Court is the version of the victim and, by necessary implication, that of the Accused, who was not previously known to the victim. No prior enmity or motive unrelated to the immediate boundary dispute has been pleaded or proved.

---

### IV. DEFENCE EVIDENCE AND SUBMISSIONS

#### A. The Origin of the Incident

It is the Accused's case that on the day in question he was lawfully conducting his trade at his usual stall. The victim encroached upon the Accused's demarcated stall space, displacing his goods. The Accused remonstrated. The victim responded aggressively and pushed the Accused. The wooden crate was an object that the Accused, in the natural course of his trade, had within his immediate reach. He did not fetch it; he did not carry it to the scene.

#### B. Absence of Premeditation

The Defence relies on the fact that:

- There was no prior relationship between the parties;
- There was no prior quarrel or plan;
- The encounter was spontaneous, arising at a public market in the ordinary course of business;
- The instrument used was one immediately to hand, and not one selected or carried for the purpose.

These circumstances are consistent with a sudden flare of temper in the heat of a market dispute and inconsistent with any deliberate, pre-meditated infliction of grievous hurt.

#### C. The Nature of the Injury

While the fracture of an arm unquestionably constitutes "grievous hurt" within the meaning of Section 320 of the Penal Code, the Defence respectfully invites the Court to consider:

- The injury was caused by a single blow;
- The victim was treated and discharged after ten days;
- There is no medical evidence before the Court of any permanent disability, deformity, or grievous injury of the severity contemplated by any of the seven clauses of Section 320.

---

### V. LEGAL SUBMISSIONS

#### A. The Intention Required under Section 324

To secure a conviction under Section 324, the Prosecution must prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that the Accused **voluntarily** caused grievous hurt — that is to say, that he either:

- intended to cause grievous hurt; or
- knew that his act was likely to cause grievous hurt; or
- intended to cause hurt, and the hurt actually caused is grievous (third limb of Section 299, applied through Section 320).

*See* the celebrated formulation in our courts that the prosecution must establish the "intention or knowledge" in the mind of the accused at the time of the act. Where the prosecution's case rests solely on the inference of intention from a single blow struck in sudden provocation, the chain must be unbroken.

#### B. The Fourth Exception to Section 300 — Sudden Quarrel

The Defence does **not** concede that this is a homicide, and accordingly the Fourth Exception to Section 300 is not strictly invoked. However, the principles of law pertaining to the **heat of passion upon sudden quarrel** are of clear persuasive and analogous value in assessing the *mens rea* under Section 324.

Our courts have consistently held that where an act is done in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without premeditation, the gravity of the offence is materially reduced. As the Supreme Court has observed, in such cases the accused's capacity for deliberation is suspended, and the act must be judged accordingly.

*See in principle*: **Don Martin Singho v. The Queen** (1963) 65 NLR 161, and the consistent line of authority that "sudden provocation" is a relevant circumstance bearing upon intention.

#### C. General Exception — Grave and Sudden Provocation (Section 294)

Section 294 of the Penal Code provides that culpable homicide is not murder when the offender is deprived of self-control by grave and sudden provocation. While the section is, by its terms, addressed to homicide, the principle of grave and sudden provocation reducing the *mens rea* of an accused is a recognised doctrine of general application in our criminal law.

The Defence will invite the Court to apply this principle in mitigation, in the alternative, in assessing the moral culpability of the Accused.

#### D. Right of Private Defence (Section 93)

Should the evidence disclose that the victim first assaulted the Accused by pushing him, the Defence will invite the Court to consider whether the Accused did not exceed his right of private defence of the person, contrary to Section 93 of the Penal Code. The use of a single blow, with the first object to hand, in response to an unlawful push, is unlikely to be disproportionate in the eyes of a reasonable person placed in the same circumstances.

---

### VI. MITIGATING FACTORS

Should the Court be satisfied that the offence is made out, the Defence respectfully submits the following mitigating circumstances:

1. **No prior criminal record**, if the Court be pleased to so assume in the absence of a record to the contrary;
2. **Spontaneity of the act**, with no premeditation;
3. **Provocation** by the victim in encroaching upon the Accused's stall and assaulting him;
4. **Single blow**, with no weapon selected or carried;
5. **No permanent injury** — the victim was treated and discharged in ten days;
6. **The Accused is a vendor of modest means**, supporting himself and his family through lawful trade at the market;
7. **Likely loss of livelihood** and the social stigma attaching to a market-day altercation;
8. **Remorse**, which the Accused will affirm through his testimony and unsworn statement from the dock, in accordance with Section 241 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, No. 15 of 1979.

---

### VII. PRAYER

In the circumstances, the Defence respectfully prays that this Honourable Court:

1. Acquits the Accused of the offence under Section 324 of the Penal Code on the ground that the Prosecution has not proved the requisite *mens rea* beyond reasonable doubt;
2. In the alternative, holds that the act falls within the lesser offence of voluntarily causing hurt under Section 322, or the offence under Section 326 read with the Third Exception (or analogous reduced culpability);
3. In the further alternative, in the event of conviction, takes into account the mitigating factors set out above and passes a sentence proportionate to the gravity of the conduct, having regard to the principles enunciated in **Attorney-General v. Jayasundara** and the sentencing jurisprudence of the Supreme Court;
4. Grants the Accused such further relief as this Honourable Court shall deem fit and proper.

---

**Respectfully submitted on behalf of the Accused, A. Bandara.**

[Signed]
**Counsel for the Accused**

# CLOSING ARGUMENT ON BEHALF OF THE PROSECUTION

**IN THE HIGH COURT OF THE REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA**

**Case No.: HC/ALU/2026/____**

**The State v. A. Bandara**

---

May it please Your Lordship,

I appear for the State, and on the State's behalf I now close my case against the accused, A. Bandara, who stands indicted on a charge of **voluntarily causing grievous hurt, contrary to Section 324 of the Penal Code**.

This is the moment at which the State must stand by the evidence it has led, apply the law to the facts as the Court has found them, and ask this Honourable Court to return the only verdict that the evidence will support. I shall do so in four parts: first, a brief restatement of the nature of the case; second, a review of the evidence actually led; third, an application of the law to that evidence; and fourth, a rebuttal of the principal arguments advanced on the accused's behalf, and the State's submissions on sentence.

---

## I. THE NATURE OF THE CASE

This is, in its essentials, a straightforward case. A man picked up a heavy, hard, blunt object in a public market, swung it at a fellow vendor, and broke that vendor's arm. The injury required ten days in hospital. That is the undisputed core of the matter. The Defence has been constrained, fairly and properly, to concede as much.

What the Defence has done — and one must give it credit for candour — is to accept the fact of the blow and the fact of the injury, and to invite the Court to characterise the accused's culpability in a different and lesser way. The Defence has urged upon the Court, in various formulations, that the accused should be acquitted of Section 324, convicted only of a lesser offence under Section 326, or in any event dealt with leniently on the basis of provocation, sudden quarrel, and emotional heat.

The State submits, with respect, that the evidence does not support any of those outcomes. The State submits that the charge under Section 324 is made out, that the lesser charge under Section 326 is not, and that on the question of sentence the conduct of the accused displays features which, while not elevating the matter beyond the framework of Section 324, do not warrant the indulgence the Defence seeks.

---

## II. THE EVIDENCE LED

I will not weary the Court with a long recapitulation. The evidence, in summary, is as follows.

**First**, the testimony of the two bystander witnesses, who were present at the scene, who observed the genesis of the dispute, who watched it escalate, and who saw the accused pick up a wooden crate and strike the victim with it. Their evidence was clear, consistent, and unshaken in cross-examination. The Defence has suggested that their "independence" was a matter to be tested; the Defence tested it, and the evidence stood.

**Second**, the testimony of the victim himself, who described the altercation, the blow, the immediate sensation of the fracture, and the consequences — the ten days in hospital, the pain, the lost trade, the lost income. His evidence corroborated that of the bystanders in every material particular.

**Third**, the medical evidence, which confirmed the fracture of the arm. A fracture of a bone is, by the express terms of the Seventh Clause of Section 311, "grievous hurt" within the meaning of the Code. That is a statutory classification, and it is not open to the Court to disregard it. The Defence has suggested, with respect, that the Court should somehow discount the gravity of the injury because it was treated within ten days and left no permanent disability. With the greatest respect, that is not the test. The test is whether a bone was fractured, and the answer is yes.

**Fourth**, the wooden crate itself, produced and identified, which is the weapon used. The Defence has scrutinised its chain of custody. The chain of custody was duly established.

Taken together, these four streams of evidence — eyewitness, victim, medical, and physical — converge on a single, coherent narrative. There is no material inconsistency among them. There is no suggestion of fabrication. There is no evidence of any ulterior motive on the part of the victim or the witnesses to falsely implicate the accused. The narrative that emerges is, in the State's submission, the narrative that happened.

---

## III. APPLICATION OF LAW TO FACTS

The elements of the offence under Section 324 are well settled, and I do not need to detain the Court on them at length. To secure a conviction, the State must prove:

**(a)** that the accused caused hurt to the victim;
**(b)** that the hurt so caused was grievous; and
**(c)** that the act of causing such hurt was voluntary.

I take each in turn.

### A. Causing Hurt

The first element is proved, and is in fact conceded. A wooden crate, swung with force against a human arm, is plainly capable of causing hurt, and in this case demonstrably did so. The accused caused the hurt. This is not in dispute.

### B. Grievous Hurt

The second element is proved by the medical evidence, and is also, in effect, conceded. The fracture of the arm engages the Seventh Clause of Section 311. It is "grievous hurt" as a matter of statutory definition.

The Defence has invited the Court to look behind the statutory classification and to consider the practical severity of the injury — that the victim was treated and discharged, that no permanent damage is alleged, that life goes on. The State submits, with respect, that this is not the proper inquiry. The Code, in Section 311, has set out with precision the categories of hurt that are to be treated as "grievous." A fracture is one of them. It is not for the Court to add a judicial gloss that the fracture must be of a particular kind, or accompanied by particular consequences, in order to qualify. The Legislature has spoken, and the Legislature's classification is binding.

### C. Voluntariness

The third element — voluntariness — is, on the evidence, the only one over which any real contest arises. The State submits that voluntariness is established beyond any reasonable doubt.

The accused, on his own plea and on the testimony of every witness, was conscious, in control of his actions, and aware of what he was doing. He was not in a state of automatism. He was not acting in a reflex. He was not sleepwalking. He picked up a wooden crate, raised it, and swung it at the victim. That sequence of conduct is the paradigm of a voluntary act. The State relies, in this respect, on the long-settled principle that a directed, purposeful, motor act by a conscious person is voluntary, and that the law attributes the natural and probable consequences of that act to the person who performs it.

The Defence has urged that the accused was acting in the heat of passion, in a state of emotional disturbance, having been "pushed" by the victim. The State makes two submissions in response.

**First**, even on the Defence's own version of events, the conduct of the accused was voluntary in the legal sense. A man who is angry, who feels he has been wronged, who is in a public place, and who responds by picking up a heavy object and breaking another man's arm, is not, in any sense recognised by the criminal law, a man whose act was involuntary. He is a man who chose, in the moment, to do what he did. The law does not excuse that choice merely because the choice was made under emotional pressure.

**Second**, the Defence's account of what preceded the blow — that the victim "pushed" the accused — is unsupported by any independent evidence. The two eyewitnesses did not corroborate it. The victim himself denies it. The only source for this allegation is the accused himself. Your Lordship will weigh it as such.

---

## IV. THE DEFENCE ARGUMENTS, AND WHY THEY DO NOT AVAIL

I now turn to the principal arguments advanced on the accused's behalf, and address them directly.

### A. The Argument that Section 326 Should Be Preferred to Section 324

The Defence has urged, with some force, that the proper charge on the facts is Section 326 — voluntarily causing grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation — rather than Section 324.

The State submits that Section 326 is not available on the evidence, for two reasons.

**First**, the provocation alleged is not, as a matter of law, capable of amounting to "grave and sudden provocation" within the meaning of the Code. The dispute was over a stall boundary. The accused was, on the Defence's own account, verbally remonstrated with, and possibly pushed. Even taking the Defence case at its highest, this is a disagreement about the location of goods in a market, on an ordinary day, between two working people. Our law has long recognised that words, however offensive, and minor physical confrontations, such as a push, do not constitute grave provocation for the purposes of reducing culpability for a violent response of this kind. The accused's response — to break the other man's arm with a wooden crate — was grossly disproportionate to anything that could plausibly be characterised as provocation.

**Second**, and in any event, Section 326 requires that the provocation be such as would cause a reasonable person to lose self-control. The accused's conduct — arming himself, even momentarily, with a hard wooden object, and using it with sufficient force to fracture bone — is not the conduct of a person who has merely lost self-control. It is the conduct of a person who has, in the moment, decided to inflict serious harm. The legal category of "loss of self-control" cannot be stretched to accommodate that decision.

The State accordingly submits that the Section 326 route is not available to the accused, and that the charge under Section 324 is the proper charge on the facts.

### B. The Argument from Premeditation (or the Absence of It)

The Defence has placed weight on the fact that the accused did not plan the assault, that the encounter was spontaneous, and that the wooden crate was the object to hand.

The State has no quarrel with these facts. They are, in the State's submission, irrelevant. Section 324 does not require premeditation. The offence is complete the moment a person voluntarily causes grievous hurt. Whether the hurt was planned or impulsive bears on sentence; it does not bear on guilt. A man who kills another in a sudden fit of temper is no less guilty of culpable homicide than one who lies in wait. The same principle applies, with full force, to a man who breaks another man's arm in a sudden fit of temper in a market.

The Defence is, in effect, asking the Court to elevate the absence of premeditation into a defence. The law of Sri Lanka does not recognise such a defence to a charge under Section 324. To recognise it would be to rewrite the statute, and that is not within the province of this Court.

### C. The Right of Private Defence

The Defence has alluded, in passing, to the right of private defence under Section 32 and following of the Penal Code, suggesting that the accused was responding to an unlawful push by the victim.

The State submits that this argument is not made out, on the evidence.

The right of private defence is available only where there is a reasonable apprehension of harm, and only to the extent of what is necessary to repel that harm. The accused was not, on the evidence, in any reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt from being pushed. The response — to pick up a heavy wooden object and strike the victim with sufficient force to break his arm — is wildly disproportionate to any threat that a push could possibly constitute. The right of private defence cannot be invoked to justify a retaliatory assault of this kind. To allow it would be to license any vendor in any market to beat any other vendor with whatever object is to hand, on the assertion that he was "pushed." The law does not, and cannot, tolerate that.

In any event, the factual basis for the argument is, as I have noted, unsupported by any evidence other than the accused's own assertion. The Court is not bound to accept that assertion, and on the totality of the evidence, the State submits, ought not to.

### D. The Argument from the Ten-Day Hospitalisation

The Defence has suggested that the relatively short period of hospitalisation somehow diminishes the gravity of the injury, and that this should weigh in the accused's favour.

The State has already addressed this. A fracture is a fracture. The Legislature has classified it as grievous hurt. The Court must give effect to that classification. The fact that modern medicine is able to treat fractures effectively, and to discharge patients within a relatively short period, is not a reason to treat the underlying injury as anything other than what the statute says it is.

The State notes, in passing, that the ten days in hospital represent ten days of pain, ten days of incapacity, ten days of lost trade and lost income for a working vendor. The Defence's framing of this as a mitigating circumstance is, with respect, somewhat tone-deaf to the reality of the victim's experience.

### E. The Argument from the Accused's Character

The Defence has alluded to the accused's good character, his lack of prior convictions, his position as a working vendor, and his family responsibilities. The State does not contest any of these matters, and will not oppose the leading of evidence to prove them at the appropriate stage.

The State observes, however, that good character is not a defence to a charge of this kind. It is, at most, a matter for sentence. And even at the stage of sentence, it must be weighed alongside the nature of the conduct in issue. A man of previously good character who, in a moment of ungovernable temper, breaks another man's arm in a public market, is a man of previously good character who has, on this occasion, done a serious wrong. The State trusts that this Court will keep both facts in view.

---

## V. SUBMISSIONS ON SENTENCE

Should this Court, having considered the matters above, be of the view that a conviction under Section 324 is appropriate, the State makes the following submissions on sentence, in the event that the matter proceeds to that stage.

**First**, the State submits that the offence is a serious one. A fracture of a bone, deliberately inflicted with an implement, in a public place, in the course of a commercial dispute, is not at the lower end of the spectrum of offences under Section 324. The Legislature has set a maximum of seven years' imprisonment and a fine. The State does not suggest that the maximum is appropriate, but submits that a custodial sentence, as distinct from a fine alone, is warranted. A fine alone would, in the State's submission, fail to reflect the gravity of the conduct and the public interest in deterring the use of objects as weapons in public places.

**Second**, the State submits that the circumstances of the assault — the use of an implement, the force employed, the location in a crowded public market where bystanders, including children, might have been struck — are aggravating features that this Court should weigh.

**Third**, the State notes that the accused has, in effect, contested the charge throughout these proceedings, has declined to accept responsibility in any meaningful way, and has put the victim to the burden of proving what was, in substance, conceded. That is his right, and the State does not criticise him for exercising it. But it is a matter that this Court may properly take into account when considering whether, and to what extent, the accused has shown the remorse to which the Defence alluded in opening.

**Fourth**, the State accepts that the accused has no recorded prior convictions, and that this is a first offence. That is a matter properly to be weighed in his favour.

**Fifth**, the State submits that compensation to the victim, by way of a fine or otherwise, is appropriate. The victim is a working vendor who lost ten days of trade through no fault of his own. The Court may consider, in addition to any custodial component, an order that the accused pay compensation under the provisions of the **Code of Criminal Procedure Act, No. 15 of 1979**, and in particular the powers of the Court in that regard.

---

## VI. THE STATE'S PRAYER

In all the circumstances, the State prays that this Honourable Court:

1. **Return a finding of guilt** against the accused, A. Bandara, on the charge of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, contrary to Section 324 of the Penal Code;

2. **Decline to substitute** a conviction under Section 326, for the reasons set out above;

3. **Pass sentence** that reflects the gravity of the offence, the circumstances of its commission, the harm done to the victim, and the matters personal to the accused that the Defence has placed on the record, including — to the extent the Court is so satisfied — his lack of prior convictions and his circumstances as a working man with family responsibilities;

4. **Consider an order for compensation** to the victim, in addition to or as part of any sentence imposed.

The State is conscious that sentencing is a matter for the discretion of this Court, and trusts that this Court will exercise that discretion with the care and the balance that the law requires.

---

## VII. CONCLUSION

May it please Your Lordship, this is, in the end, a case about a man who used a wooden crate to break another man's arm. The evidence of that fact is clear, consistent, and uncontradicted. The medical record confirms the gravity of the injury. The legal classification of the injury as "grievous" is statutory, and is not in doubt. The voluntariness of the act is established by the very nature of what occurred.

The Defence has asked this Court to look behind the obvious facts and to find, in the heat of the moment, in the trivial nature of the underlying dispute, in the accused's lack of prior convictions, and in the disproportion between the maximum sentence and the conduct, a reason to characterise the matter in a lesser way. The State has great sympathy for the human realities behind every criminal case, and for the difficult position in which the accused now finds himself. But the State's duty is to apply the law to the facts as the Court finds them, and not to be deflected from that duty by considerations of sympathy.

The law of Sri Lanka does not excuse the breaking of another man's bones, on a public market day, simply because the breaker was angry, or because the dispute that triggered his anger was trivial, or because no one planned the assault in advance. If the law were otherwise, the streets and markets of this country would not be safe for working people going about their lawful business. This Court has an opportunity, in its judgment in this case, to affirm that the use of objects as weapons against the person is a serious matter, and that those who commit such acts will be held to account under the law that the Legislature has enacted.

The State accordingly invites this Honourable Court to return a verdict of guilty on the charge under Section 324 of the Penal Code.

I am obliged, Your Lordship.

**State Counsel**
*For the Prosecution*
*High Court of Sri Lanka*

# CLOSING ARGUMENT ON BEHALF OF THE DEFENCE

**IN THE HIGH COURT OF THE REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA**

**Case No.: HC/ALU/2026/____**

**The State v. A. Bandara**

---

May it please Your Lordship,

I appear for the accused, A. Bandara. I have listened with care and with respect to the learned State Counsel, whose submission was as able as it was firmly put. The Defence does not complain of the force of the arguments advanced against the accused. The Defence asks only that this Honourable Court weigh those arguments, in their full force, against the evidence actually led, against the law as it stands, and against the fundamental presumption of innocence to which every accused in this country is entitled.

I shall structure this closing in four parts. First, I will restate, plainly, what is conceded and what is not. Second, I will address the proper construction of Section 324 and the burden that rests on the State at every stage. Third, I will take the State's principal arguments in turn, and show why, with respect, they do not bear the weight that has been placed upon them. Fourth, I will address the question of sentence, and the matters that this Court is invited to weigh if — and only if — it finds the charge made out.

---

## I. WHAT IS CONCEDED, AND WHAT IS NOT

The Defence has been candid from the outset, and will remain so. Let me restate the concessions clearly.

The Defence concedes:

- That a dispute arose between the accused and the complainant at the market, over a stall boundary.
- That the accused struck the complainant with a wooden crate.
- That the complainant sustained a fracture of the arm.
- That the complainant was hospitalised for ten days and then discharged.

The Defence does **not** concede:

- That the accused possessed the mental state required for an offence under Section 324 of the Penal Code.
- That the conduct of the accused, properly characterised in law, falls within Section 324 rather than within Section 326.
- That the defence of grave and sudden provocation is, on the evidence, foreclosed.
- That the State has discharged the burden of proof that rests upon it throughout these proceedings.

The State has framed its closing around a single rhetorical proposition: that this is "a case about a man who used a wooden crate to break another man's arm." The Defence accepts the antecedent, but denies the consequent. The fact that an arm was broken does not, of itself, conclude the legal analysis. It concludes one factual question — the question whether grievous hurt was caused — and leaves open every other question of equal or greater importance. The State has, in the Defence submission, allowed the force of the fact of injury to carry it past questions of law and fact that the Court is bound to consider separately.

---

## II. THE BURDEN OF PROOF, AND THE LIMITS OF INFERENCE

The Defence begins, as it began in opening, with the burden of proof.

The burden of proving every element of the offence under Section 324 rests, at all times, upon the State. That burden is not discharged by the accumulation of facts that are, individually, consistent with guilt. The burden is to prove, **beyond reasonable doubt**, that the accused *voluntarily caused grievous hurt* in the legal sense of those words — that is to say, with the mental state that the law requires.

The State has, in its closing, invited the Court to draw inferences of intention from the weapon used and the injury caused. The Defence does not contest that intention may, in a proper case, be inferred from conduct. But the inference must be a proper one, drawn from a proper basis, and it must be the only reasonable inference available. Where the evidence leaves open a reasonable possibility that the accused did not possess the requisite mental state, the accused is entitled to the benefit of that possibility, and the State has failed to discharge its burden.

In this case, the inference the State asks the Court to draw is that the accused, in swinging the crate, either intended to cause grievous hurt, or knew that grievous hurt was likely. The Defence submits that the evidence does not support that inference, and that a reasonable alternative explanation is not only available but is, on the totality of the evidence, the more compelling inference.

What is that alternative? It is the inference that the accused, in a sudden flare of temper, in a public place, in the course of a heated and unwelcome dispute over his livelihood, did an angry and harmful thing — an act for which the law provides, in Section 326, a proper and proportionate response. To elevate that act into a Section 324 offence requires evidence of a mental state that this Court has not been shown to exist.

The State has said, more than once, that the accused "armed himself" with a wooden crate. With respect, that is a piece of advocacy dressed up as a finding of fact. The accused did not arm himself. He did not fetch a weapon. He did not pause, consider, and select. He used, in the heat of the moment, an object that was at hand, in a place where such objects are routinely to hand, in the course of a sudden quarrel. The State's characterisation of that conduct is not an inference of fact; it is an argument, and the Court must judge it as such.

---

## III. THE STATE'S ARGUMENTS, ADDRESSED

I now turn to the principal arguments advanced by the State, and address each in turn.

### A. The Argument that Voluntariness Is Plainly Established

The State submits that voluntariness is, in effect, conceded, because the accused picked up an object and swung it. The Defence accepts that the act of striking the complainant was a voluntary act in the narrow sense that it was a conscious, directed motor act. The Defence does **not** accept that the bare fact of a voluntary physical act discharges the State's burden in respect of the **offence charged**.

The voluntariness required by Section 324 is not merely the voluntariness of the bodily movement. It is the voluntariness of the *causing of grievous hurt* — which is to say, the State must prove that the accused's voluntary conduct was accompanied by the mental state that the law requires. A man can voluntarily strike another, in a moment of blind rage, without either intending to cause grievous hurt or knowing that grievous hurt is likely. The law distinguishes between these cases, and the State cannot collapse that distinction by the simple expedient of repeating the word "voluntary."

The State has also, in its closing, made much of the assertion that the accused was "in control" of his actions. The Defence submits that this, too, is advocacy rather than evidence. The accused was, no doubt, conscious. He was, no doubt, capable of bodily movement. Whether he was in the calm possession of his reflective faculties, surveying his options and selecting the one that would break the complainant's arm, is a different question — and it is a question on which the evidence is silent, or at best divided. The Defence will return to this in the context of Section 326.

### B. The Argument that the Injury Is Grievous Hurt as a Matter of Statute

The State relies on the Seventh Clause of Section 311, and submits that a fracture of a bone is, by force of the statute, "grievous hurt." The Defence accepts that a fracture of a bone is, *prima facie*, grievous hurt within the statutory definition. The Defence does not contest this.

What the Defence contests is the further proposition, implicit in the State's argument, that the statutory classification is the end of the matter. It is not. The statutory classification establishes that the hurt, *as a matter of physical fact*, is of the kind that the law treats as grievous. It does not establish *which offence* the conduct falls within. That is a separate question, governed by the mental state of the accused, and answered by reference to the relevant provisions of the Code — including Section 326.

The State treats the grievous nature of the injury as the decisive factor in the case. The Defence treats it as one fact among several, which must be weighed alongside the mental state of the accused, the circumstances of the assault, and the question of which provision of the Code properly applies. On that weighing, the State has not made out its case for Section 324.

### C. The Argument that Section 326 Is Not Available

The State submits, in two limbs, that Section 326 is not available. I will take each in turn.

**First**, the State submits that the provocation alleged is not "grave" within the meaning of the Code. The Defence accepts that the dispute was, in its origin, a commercial one. The Defence submits, however, that the gravity of provocation is not to be measured by reference to the subject matter of the dispute in the abstract, but by reference to its effect upon the person provoked, in the circumstances in which he found himself.

The accused is a working vendor. His stall is his livelihood. The boundary of that stall is not, to him, a triviality; it is the difference between earning a day's wage and not earning it. The dispute arose suddenly, in a public place, in circumstances of commercial pressure. A reasonable person in the accused's position, suddenly confronted with what he perceived as an unjustified encroachment upon his means of livelihood, in a crowded and emotionally charged environment, could well have been deprived of self-control. The law does not require that the provocation be objectively extraordinary; it requires that it be grave and sudden in its effect upon a reasonable person in the accused's circumstances.

**Second**, the State submits that the accused's conduct was too deliberate to constitute a loss of self-control. The State argues that a man who picks up a heavy object and uses it with sufficient force to break a bone is not a man who has lost self-control. The Defence has two responses.

The first is factual. The accused's conduct, as the Court has heard it, was a single blow, struck in a moment of anger, with an object to hand. It was not a sustained assault. It was not a series of blows. It was not a premeditated or measured use of force. The State's characterisation of it as "the conduct of a person who has, in the moment, decided to inflict serious harm" is, with respect, an overstatement of what the evidence discloses.

The second is legal. The cases on Section 326 — and the analogous cases on the Fourth Exception to Section 300 — recognise that the manner of a provoked assault may itself be heated, uncontrolled, and disproportionate to the provocation, without thereby removing the case from the scope of the provision. The law does not require that a provoked man strike his provoker with measured restraint. It requires that the provocation be grave and sudden, that the accused be deprived of self-control by it, and that the act be done before the accused has had time to regain that self-control. Those requirements, on the evidence, are met.

The Defence accordingly submits that Section 326 is the proper charge on these facts, and that the accused should be acquitted of Section 324 and convicted of the lesser offence.

### D. The Argument from the Alleged Push

The State makes much of the fact that the alleged push by the complainant is not corroborated by independent evidence, and that the complainant denies it. The Defence accepts that the question of who struck or pushed whom first is a difficult one, on the evidence, and that the Court must weigh the competing accounts with care.

What the Defence submits, however, is that the question is not decisive. Whether or not the complainant pushed the accused, the fact remains that the dispute was sudden, the accused was put in a position of emotional stress, and his response was an immediate, unpremeditated blow. The push, if it occurred, is part of the provocation; if it did not occur, the verbal and commercial provocation remains. Either way, the case for Section 326 — and against Section 324 — is made out.

The Defence further notes that the State's closing treats the alleged push as the linchpin of the private defence argument, and then characterises the private defence argument as "wildly disproportionate." The Defence submits that this is, with respect, a misdirection. The private defence argument is one strand of the Defence case, not the whole of it. The Defence's primary position is that the conduct falls within Section 326, regardless of the question of who pushed whom. The Court is not obliged to accept the push in order to accept the broader Defence case.

### E. The Argument from the Public Setting

The State submits that the public setting of the assault — a crowded market, with bystanders and possibly children present — is an aggravating circumstance. The Defence accepts that the public setting is a matter the Court may properly take into account. The Defence observes, however, that the very fact that the accused was in a public place, surrounded by witnesses, is a factor telling against premeditation and against the kind of deliberate, calculated conduct that Section 324 contemplates. A man who chooses to inflict grievous hurt does not, ordinarily, do so in a market in full view of dozens of potential witnesses. The accused did so, and the most natural explanation is that he was not, in that moment, choosing anything; he was reacting.

### F. The Argument on Sentence

The State has made submissions on sentence, addressed to a custodial outcome. The Defence will address sentence in due course, and at the appropriate stage. For the moment, the Defence observes only that the State has urged an approach that would, in effect, treat the accused's decision to defend himself as a circumstance telling against him at the sentencing stage. The Defence submits that the right of an accused to contest the charge — to require the State to prove its case, and to insist on the proper application of the law — is not a matter that can be held against him when sentence falls to be passed. To hold otherwise would be to penalise the exercise of a constitutional right.

---

## IV. THE MENTAL ELEMENT, RESTATED

The Defence wishes to say, with care and at length, why the question of the mental element is, in this case, the central question.

Section 324 of the Penal Code is not, despite the way the State has presented its case, a strict liability offence. It requires proof of a *mens rea* — a guilty mind. The State must prove, beyond reasonable doubt, that the accused either intended to cause grievous hurt, or knew that grievous hurt was likely to be caused. The State has not, in the Defence submission, proved either limb.

The State has not proved that the accused intended to cause grievous hurt. The accused, by his own account and on the totality of the evidence, was a man in a sudden quarrel, who lost his temper, and who struck out with the object nearest to him. A man in that state does not form the intention to cause grievous hurt. He forms, at most, the intention to hit — to retaliate, to hurt, to silence, to express his anger through his body rather than his words. That is a different mental state, and it is one that the law recognises as falling within a different and lesser category.

The State has not proved that the accused knew that grievous hurt was likely. The accused is not, on the evidence, a man of medical training. He is a working vendor, in a market, in a moment of anger. The Defence does not accept that a man in that position, swinging a wooden crate in the heat of a sudden quarrel, must be taken to have known that he was likely to break a bone. The State has not called expert evidence to that effect. The State has not pointed to any feature of the accused's conduct — the number of blows, the targeted striking of a vulnerable part of the body, the use of a particularly dangerous weapon — that would support such an inference. The inference the State asks the Court to draw is, in the Defence submission, an inference of convenience rather than of fact.

Where the State has not proved the mental element of the offence charged, the accused must be acquitted of that offence. He may, on the same facts, be convicted of a lesser offence — and the Defence submits that Section 326 is the proper lesser offence. But he may not be convicted of Section 324 on the basis of an inference that the evidence does not support.

---

## V. THE DEFENCE'S POSITION ON SENTENCE

If — and the Defence emphasises the conditional — this Court is of the view that a conviction is appropriate, the Defence makes the following submissions on sentence.

**First**, the Defence submits that a non-custodial sentence, or a short custodial sentence suspended for a period, is appropriate in this case. The accused is a man of previously good character, with no recorded prior convictions. The incident was a single blow, in a moment of heat, over a commercial dispute. The injury, while serious in classification, was treated within ten days, and left no permanent disability. The accused is a working man, with family responsibilities, whose livelihood depends on his ability to trade at the market. A custodial sentence, in these circumstances, would visit upon the accused and his family a punishment disproportionate to the conduct.

**Second**, the Defence submits that the Court may properly consider the imposition of a compensation order, under the powers conferred by the Code of Criminal Procedure Act, in lieu of, or in addition to, any other sentence. Such an order would serve the legitimate interest of the complainant in being made whole for his loss, without the destructive consequences of imprisonment for the accused and his dependants.

**Third**, the Defence submits that any sentence imposed should reflect the legislative recognition, embodied in Section 326 itself, that the conduct here is differently situated from conduct falling squarely within Section 324. Section 326 carries a lower maximum penalty than Section 324. The Legislature has, in effect, told the Courts that the provoked offender stands in a different moral position from the unprovoked one. This Court is bound to give effect to that legislative judgment.

**Fourth**, the Defence submits that the accused is entitled to have taken into account, in mitigation, the matters set out in opening: his lack of prior convictions, his character, his family responsibilities, his contribution to the economic life of his community, and the genuine remorse that he has expressed, and will continue to express, for the harm he has caused to the complainant.

---

## VI. THE DEFENCE'S PRAYER

In all the circumstances, the Defence respectfully prays that this Honourable Court:

1. **Acquit** the accused of the charge under Section 324 of the Penal Code, on the ground that the State has failed to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, the mental element required for that offence;

2. **In the alternative**, hold that the conduct of the accused falls within the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt on provocation, contrary to Section 326 of the Penal Code, and convict him of that lesser offence;

3. **In the further alternative**, in the event of conviction under Section 324, take into account the mitigating factors set out in opening and in this closing, and pass a sentence that is proportionate to the conduct, the offender, and the harm caused;

4. **Consider** the imposition of a compensation order in favour of the complainant, in lieu of or in addition to any other sentence;

5. **Grant** the accused such further and other relief as this Honourable Court shall deem fit and proper in the circumstances.

---

## VII. CONCLUSION

May it please Your Lordship, this is a case in which a man lost his temper, in a public place, over a matter of immediate concern to his livelihood, and broke another man's arm. That is a serious matter, and the accused does not seek to minimise it. He caused real harm to a real person, and he must answer for it.

But the law of this country does not require him to answer for it under Section 324. The law of this country provides, in Section 326, a different and more proportionate response to conduct of this kind — conduct that is grave, that is harmful, that deserves punishment, but that is also, in the eyes of the Legislature, differently situated from the unprovoked, deliberate infliction of grievous hurt.

This Court is not asked to excuse the accused. This Court is asked to characterise his conduct correctly. The Defence submits that the correct characterisation is not Section 324, but Section 326, and that the correct outcome is a conviction on the lesser charge, with a sentence that reflects the conduct, the harm, and the man.

The Defence accordingly invites this Honourable Court to return a verdict of not guilty on the charge under Section 324, and to proceed, if so advised, on the basis of Section 326.

I am obliged, Your Lordship.

**Respectfully submitted on behalf of the Accused, A. Bandara.**

**Defense Counsel**
*For the Accused*
*High Court of Sri Lanka*

The charge is voluntarily causing grievous hurt, contrary to Penal Code s.324. Section 324 requires the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused (i) caused hurt (s.314) and (ii) that the hurt was grievous (s.322), and (iii) that the act was voluntary in the sense that the accused possessed the requisite mens rea — intention to cause grievous hurt, or knowledge that grievous hurt was likely. As the Court of Appeal held in King v. Perera, a fracture of a bone constitutes grievous hurt under s.322, but where the harm is inflicted in the course of a sudden fight without premeditation, the mitigating framework may be engaged; the burden of proof remains on the prosecution throughout (see also Silva v. AG on the standard for circumstantial proof). On the facts: (a) The causing of hurt is conceded. (b) The grievous nature of the hurt is established by the hospital record of a fractured arm, which directly engages the 'fracture or dislocation of a bone' clause of s.322. (c) Voluntariness in the narrow sense — that the accused performed a conscious, directed motor act — is also conceded; the accused picked up a crate and struck the victim. The real contest is over the mental element. The prosecution's case on mens rea rests on inference from the weapon and the resulting fracture. While such an inference is permissible, it is not, on this record, the only reasonable inference available. The accused's account — that the blow was struck in a sudden quarrel, with an object to hand, in a moment of heated loss of self-control — is not excluded by the prosecution evidence. The bystander evidence, as led, speaks to the act of striking but does not, on the record before me, definitively establish that the accused formed the specific intention to cause grievous hurt or knew that grievous hurt was likely. Given the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt, and the principle in King v. Perera that a sudden quarrel engages the mitigating framework, I am not satisfied that the prosecution has negatived the reasonable possibility that the accused's conduct falls within s.326 (voluntarily causing grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation) rather than s.324. However, the prosecution has not formally tendered a s.326 charge, and the record contains no judicial admission or plea to s.326. A court cannot convict of an offence not charged, even as a lesser alternative, without a proper amendment or alternative charge. The proper course is therefore to decline to convict on the s.324 charge as presented, on the ground that the mental element has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. In the result, the accused is entitled to be found not guilty of s.324 on the present record. I express no view on whether a properly framed s.326 charge could be sustained, as it is not before me.

judgment.dissent_notes: I have marked this as 'not_guilty' with the insufficient_evidence flag set, because the prosecution has not, on the record as actually led, proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused possessed the mental state required for s.324. The case is a close one: the voluntary striking with a hard object causing a fracture is strongly suggestive of the s.324 mens rea, and the King v. Perera principle does not require premeditation. A court differently persuaded as to the strength of the inference of intention or knowledge from the weapon and the injury could, on this same record, properly convict under s.324, particularly if it took the view that the accused's act of arming himself with a wooden crate, even momentarily, was itself evidence of an intention to inflict serious harm. Perera squarely recognises that a sudden quarrel engages the mitigating framework; and (d) the burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt, as reaffirmed in Silva v. AG, requires more than the inference on which the State has relied. s.324: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt. Whoever voluntarily causes
grievous hurt shall be punished with imprisonment of either description
for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to
fine.

s.322: Grievous hurt. Hurt is grievous when it causes permanent loss of
sight or hearing, permanent disfigurement, fracture or dislocation of a
bone, or any hurt which endangers life or causes the sufferer to be
during the space of twenty days in severe bodily pain or unable to follow
his ordinary pursuits.

s.314: Hurt. Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person
is said to cause hurt.

Penal Code, s.328
s.328: Assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation.
Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person otherwise than on
grave and sudden provocation commits a simple offence punishable as
prescribed.

Penal Code, s.327
s.327: Criminal force. Whoever intentionally uses force to any person,
without that person's consent, in order to the committing of any offence,
or intending by the use of such force to cause injury, fear or annoyance,
commits the offence of using criminal force.

Penal Code, s.326
s.326: Assault. Whoever makes any gesture, or prepares anything, intending
that the gesture or thing shall be used against the person of another, or
knowing it to be likely that it will be so used, commits an assault.
